_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 590 words, six questions in text order: detail, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase and a final question linking the ending to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Notes in the margins
subtitle: For almost twenty years, bookseller Ambrose Kettle has been hiding handwritten notes inside the books he sells. Priya Lal went to find out why.

cards.text: Kettle & Daughter Books is so narrow that two customers cannot pass each other without one of them stepping into the poetry section. There is no daughter, Ambrose Kettle tells me cheerfully; he simply thought the name sounded more reliable. What the shop does have is a secret, although not a very well-kept one. Inside almost every book on its crowded shelves, somewhere between the pages, is a small card in Ambrose's handwriting. Some contain a single sentence. Others fill both sides. None of them is signed, and Ambrose never mentions them when he takes your money.
cards.question: What does the writer say about the name of the shop?
choices: It was already the name when Ambrose bought the shop.
Ambrose chose it to give customers a good impression.
It refers to a daughter who no longer works there.
It confuses customers who are looking for poetry.
cards.highlight: he simply thought the name sounded more reliable
cards.why: There is no daughter: 'he simply thought the name sounded more reliable'. The poetry section is only mentioned to show how narrow the shop is.

cards.text: The habit began in his first winter, when business was so slow that he had time to read most of his own stock. He found himself wanting to argue with the books, or to recommend them to someone. Since there was nobody in the shop to talk to, he wrote to whoever would buy them next. 'The first note said something like, "The ending is terrible, but stay for chapter six,"' he recalls. 'I felt slightly foolish. Then a woman came back a month later, waving the card, and asked if I had any more books like chapter six.'
cards.question: What can we infer about Ambrose's first note?
choices: It had a more positive effect than he had expected.
It was intended as a joke for a friend.
It persuaded the woman not to finish the book.
It contained criticism he later regretted.
cards.highlight: Then a woman came back a month later, waving the card
cards.why: He 'felt slightly foolish', yet the woman came back 'waving the card' and wanting more, so it worked better than he thought. She read chapter six, so she did finish.

cards.text: Nowadays, many customers come in specifically for the notes. Regulars compare them online, one woman claims to have collected more than three hundred, and a local teacher uses them with her students to start discussions. Ambrose finds this flattering but also a little worrying. He never wanted the notes to become more important than the books they sit in. That is why he keeps them anonymous and refuses to sell them separately, despite several offers. 'If someone buys a novel just for my card,' he says, 'I've failed. It's supposed to be a door, not a room.'
cards.question: What does 'It' refer to in 'It's supposed to be a door, not a room'?
choices: the novel that a customer buys
the shop itself
the discussions in the teacher's class
each note that Ambrose writes
cards.highlight: I've failed. It's supposed to be a door, not a room.
cards.why: 'It' is 'my card': a note should lead the reader into the book, not be the destination. The novel is the 'room' the card opens onto.

cards.text: Not all the notes are about the books. Some are small pieces of advice, others are jokes, and a few simply describe the weather on the day he wrote them. Last year Ambrose received a letter from a man in Canada who had bought a travel guide in the shop as a student, nearly twenty years earlier. Inside was a note saying, 'Go before you feel ready.' The man had kept it in his wallet ever since, and wrote to say that he had finally made the journey, nineteen years late. Ambrose keeps the letter pinned above the till.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the letter from Canada?
choices: to show that the shop has become famous abroad
to suggest that travel guides sell better than novels
to show how much a short note can mean to a reader over time
to show that customers often ignore Ambrose's advice
cards.highlight: The man had kept it in his wallet ever since
cards.why: The man 'had kept it in his wallet ever since', so four words stayed with him for years. He went late but he did go, so he did not ignore the advice.

cards.text: Writing the notes takes far more time than it should, and Ambrose's accountant has stopped asking about it. He reads every book before it goes on a shelf, or at least enough of it to say something honest. He refuses to praise a book he did not enjoy, which has led to some awkward conversations with local authors. 'I'm not going to pretend,' he says. 'Once you start writing what people want to hear, the whole thing loses its point.' His notes, he insists, are not reviews. They are more like a quiet word over the reader's shoulder.
cards.question: What does Ambrose mean by 'a quiet word over the reader's shoulder'?
choices: a friendly, personal comment rather than a formal judgement
a warning not to buy the book
a secret the reader must keep to themselves
a criticism of the author's writing
cards.highlight: They are more like a quiet word over the reader's shoulder.
cards.why: He says the notes 'are not reviews' but something personal, like a friend reading with you. Honest does not mean negative, so they are not mainly criticism.

cards.text: As I leave, I buy a battered collection of short stories, and Ambrose wraps it in brown paper without a word. I manage not to open it until I am on the train. The card is tucked inside the back cover, not the front, and it is not about the stories at all. 'Some secrets are better shared,' it says. 'Come back and tell me which one you liked best.' I realise then that the notes were never really a secret, or even about books. They have always been a way of keeping a conversation going.
cards.question: What does the writer realise at the end of the article?
choices: Ambrose had written the note especially for her visit.
Ambrose would prefer customers to keep his notes secret.
The notes are mainly Ambrose's way of staying in touch with his readers.
The notes are more interesting than the books.
cards.highlight: They have always been a way of keeping a conversation going.
cards.why: The 'secret' from the opening paragraph turns out to be 'a way of keeping a conversation going'. The card says secrets 'are better shared', not kept.
